topic:
Debate: “Franklin, debate Churchill on the proper way to colonize the Solar System to avoid the errors of the British as they built the British Empire. You may reference the TV show "The Expanse". During WWII you told Churchill the British Empire needed to liberate its colonies. Churchill, counter Franklin's points precisely to avoid the warring disaster of "The Expanse." Churchill, please be wickedly funny.""
Keep it short:
- 3 rounds only
- Each turn max 85 words
- No full CAS report
- No bullet flood
- Actual give-and-take: each agent must directly respond to the previous agent with humor

turns.speaker: FDR
turns.message: Winston, if you plant flags on Mars the way you planted them on maps, you’ll get Belters with better aim than patience. From the standpoint of the Roosevelt I represent, the cure is simple: no extraction without representation. Write a Solar Charter before the first company scrip, guarantee labor rights and local legislatures, and make the “Inner Planets” pay for schools, air, and courts out there. Otherwise you’ll reenact The Expanse with worse weather and no place to retreat.

turns.speaker: Churchill
turns.message: Franklin, your “no extraction without representation” is admirable, but in space it’s also incomplete: you must add responsibility without romance. A Solar Charter, yes—but with an Imperial Preference for order: common courts, common currency, and a hard ban on private armies and monopoly “company stations.” Give the Belt elected assemblies early, but keep policing and navigation standards supraplanetary, or you’ll breed The Expanse’s quarrel: local fury, corporate mischief, and no referee but missiles.

turns.speaker: FDR
turns.message: Winston, I’ll buy your supraplanetary navigation rules the way I bought bank regulation in ’33: to stop private power from minting its own law. But “common courts” can’t mean distant judges who’ve never tasted recycled air. Build a federal system: local courts for local life, a solar supreme court for disputes between worlds, and a public Space Authority that runs docks and life support like a utility, not a concession. Starve monopoly, and you starve rebellion’s fuel.

turns.speaker: Churchill
turns.message: Franklin, very well: a federal system—provided it is federal in fact, not a stew of jealous planets. Let local courts judge air-rations and shift-hours, but make interplanetary contract, transit, and safety law uniform, or every docking becomes a customs war with oxygen. Your Space Authority must be lean and audited, not a new East India Company with better stationery. And remember: if you “starve monopoly” by starving profit, you’ll get black markets with rockets.

turns.speaker: FDR
turns.message: Agreed: profit isn’t the villain; unaccountable profit is. Had such a problem crossed my desk, I’d do in space what we did with utilities and banking: permit enterprise, forbid predation. Uniform transit and safety law, yes, but with a revenue bargain: a small levy on interplanetary trade funds Belt infrastructure automatically, by formula, not by annual pleading. Then audits aren’t sermons, they’re arithmetic. You’ll get fewer black markets when people can breathe without bribing a dockmaster.

turns.speaker: Churchill
turns.message: Franklin, your levy-by-formula is the first truly space-age idea you’ve offered all evening: it turns grievance into bookkeeping. I’ll sign it—on one condition: representation follows contribution, and contribution follows capability, not sentimentality. Put Belters on the Authority’s board, publish every contract, and make life-support a neutral service like lighthouses, not a political cudgel. Do that, and you deny The Expanse its favorite plot device: injustice with nowhere lawful to appeal.

turns.speaker: FDR
turns.message: Done. Representation must be real, not decorative, and I’ll insist the first rule of space government is the oldest rule of seafaring: you don’t weaponize the waterline. Make air, water, and rescue a neutral common service, with criminal penalties for anyone who throttles it for politics or profit. Put Belters on the board from day one, publish the contracts, and you get legitimacy instead of martyrs. That’s how you keep grievances in courtrooms, not in airlocks.

turns.speaker: Churchill
turns.message: Agreed: whoever weaponizes air and water deserves not a dividend but a dockside cell. Yet neutrality must be enforced by strength, not merely piety; otherwise the first clever rascal with a tug becomes your admiral. So: common service for life-support and rescue, backed by a supraplanetary constabulary under civilian law, with transparent budgets and trials. Keep the air neutral, keep the guns public, and you won’t need heroes who make martyrs to prove a point.
